Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify causes of degenerative joint disease in the knee beyond primary osteoarthritis.
Review nonsurgical and non-arthroplasty treatment options for these other conditions.
List indications for total knee arthroplasty, and identify the surgical technique best used to
manage each specific disease process.
Differentiate the perioperative management, surgical risks, and outcomes of primary
osteoarthritis for each of these indications.
Degenerative Arthritis of the Knee


Degenerative Arthritis of the Knee
Degenerative arthritis of the knee involves any process that may lead to wear and
destruction of the intact cartilaginous structures or underlying subchondral bone about
the knee. Although primary osteoarthritis is the most common etiology for degenerative
knee disease, degenerative wear and disease may develop in a knee for various other
reasons, including extra-articular deformity, inflammatory arthritis, tumors,
osteonecrosis, sepsis, and trauma. These disease processes may lead to end-stage
arthritic changes, resulting in the need for total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
Extra-articular Deformities

Background
An extra-articular deformity is a uniplanar or multiplanar deformity resulting from some
type of angular deformity or deformation outside of the periarticular femur or tibia. It
commonly results from previous trauma, such as a previous femur or tibia fracture. It
also may result from a growth disturbance or growth abnormality. This deformity away
from the site of the joint may lead to eccentric or abnormal joint forces, which, with time,
may lead to further degeneration of the joint surfaces.
Extra-articular deformities are a somewhat uncommon cause of degenerative joint
disease in modern TKA because surgical management of fractures or deformities has
become more common. In the past, when nonsurgical management of long bone
fractures was more of an accepted treatment option, a higher incidence of extra-
articular deformities leading to progressive degenerative arthritis were observed.
Advances in skeletal trauma management via intramedullary fixation have led to better
union rates, less soft-tissue stripping, and faster mobilization. Secondary deformities
have been more aggressively managed via osteotomies and/or deformity correction with
external fixation techniques.

Surgical Management
Nonarthroplasty Techniques
Bracing
Osteotomy

Nonarthroplasty Techniques
Depending on the extent of the deformity, nonsurgical management may involve
stabilizing braces that attempt to modify or correct the deformity or off-load the arthritic
part of the joint. Specialized braces, such as unloader braces or variations of a hip-knee-
ankle-foot orthosis, occasionally may be helpful. Shoe modifications may be helpful in
limited circumstances.
Occasionally, nonarthroplasty surgical techniques, such as osteotomy, may be indicated.
The surgeon may consider a corrective osteotomy to correct the extra-articular
deformity at the location of the fracture malunion or growth disturbance. Alternatively, a
distal femur osteotomy or a high tibial osteotomy may be indicated to off-load the
degenerative compartment of the joint.
Arthroplasty Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Imaging
Preoperative planning should include long-leg coronal and sagittal radiographs to determine
the location and extent of the deformity and plan for correction at the time of TKA. Cross-
sectional imaging studies may be considered if substantial axial deformity is anticipated
based on the physical examination or radiographic findings (Figure 1).

Figure 1
Standing bilateral long-leg (A), AP left knee (B), and lateral left knee (C) radiographs demonstrate
preoperative planning for the management of extra-articular deformities. (Courtesy of Jeffrey A.
Geller MD, New York, NY.)
Reconstructive options
Extra-articular deformities present a difficult technical challenge in attempting to restore the
mechanical axis. Reconstructive options include the following:
A one-stage procedure, in which TKA is performed with correction of the extra-articular
deformity.
A one-stage procedure, in which an extra-articular correctional osteotomy is performed at
the time of index TKA.
A two-stage procedure, in which an extra-articular correctional osteotomy is performed
several months before the primary TKA and allowed to heal.
Intra-articular correction
For less severe extra-articular deformities, appropriate intra-articular bone cuts can be
planned to restore alignment, and the necessary soft-tissue releases can be performed to
balance the knee in flexion and extension. These types of intra-articular compensatory
corrections can be more readily performed if the extra-articular deformity is distant from the
joint and if preoperative templating demonstrates that the planned bony cuts do not
interfere with ligamentous attachments.
Extra-articular correction

In patients with severe extra-articular deformities, one- or two-stage extra-articular
correctional osteotomies may be required.
Location of the deformity
The center of the deformity often guides surgical management because as it moves further
away from the knee, its effect on the mechanical limb alignment decreases, and the
deformity becomes easier to manage via TKA.
Smaller deformities close to the knee joint may require substantial correction, whereas
larger deformities farther away may have minimal effects on bone resection and balancing
Figure 2).
Figure 2

severe effect on angulation at the knee joint. The anatomic axes and mechanical axis are shown.
Severe deviation of the mechanical axis is observed. B, AP radiograph of the right knee of the
patient shown in panel A demonstrates the tibial deformity. C, Standing bilateral long-leg

Postoperative Management
Postoperative management after TKA for extra-articular deformity typically is not different
than most standard postoperative TKA protocols.
If an osteotomy is necessary, specific weight-bearing restrictions may need to be implemented
according to general internal fixation principles.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Using technology is advantageous
The surgeon should consider nonconventional methods of surgical instrumentation, such as
computer navigation or robotic surgery, because the deformity may affect or impede the use
of traditional manual instruments. These enabling technologies may help avoid
malalignment that may be encountered because of difficulty using conventional
instrumentation.
Consider constraint
In addition, extensive planning regarding the type of implant, the level of constraint, and the
kinematic option of maintaining versus replacing the posterior cruciate ligament is essential.
If suspicion of ligamentous compromise exists, higher levels of constraint, such as varus-
valgus–constrained and even constrained TKA, should be available on the day of surgery, if
necessary.
Inflammatory response
One of the more common pitfalls after TKA for extra-articular deformity is underestimating
the inflammatory response of the knee and limb after a sizable limb alignment correction,
which leads to wound problems, swelling blisters, and potential periprosthetic joint
infections (PJIs).
Weight-bearing precautions
Advancing weight-bearing restrictions too quickly before a potential corrective osteotomy
may be fully healed may lead to early failure.

Complications
Infection, failed osteotomy fixation, wound problems, and stiffness are potential complications
in this group of patients and are related to the extensive amount of surgical trauma that may
be necessary in these types of cases and the increased amount of swelling and inflammation.
Outcomes
Overall, results may be quite good for these patients with careful preoperative planning and
surgical execution.
Several moderately sized series show good outcomes in these patients.
Demir et al1 described excellent results in a small group of patients who underwent
deformity correction at the time of TKA, reporting 90% good to excellent results.
Similarly, Loures et al2 reported favorable outcomes in a larger group of patients with the
same stage of deformity correction and TKA.
Inflammatory Arthritis of the Knee
Background
Inflammatory arthropathies of the knee include a wide spectrum of rheumatologic diseases in
which the knee joint is further degenerated based on biologic attack because of immunologic
processes.
The most common type is rheumatoid arthritis; other types include disorders such as psoriatic
arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Reiter syndrome, and other less common
inflammatory arthropathies.
Rheumatoid Arthritis
Inflammatory arthropathies often are associated with poor host bone quality because of oral
corticosteroid treatment or disuse osteopenia.
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis also may have micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia) or loss
of motion in the temporomandibular joint.
Preoperative planning in patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is imperative to ensure
that appropriately sized (small) components are available (Figure 3).

Figure 3
Standing bilateral AP knee radiographs demonstrate inflammatory arthritis/rheumatoid
arthritis with severe joint space destruction, cyst formation, minimal angular deformity, and
lack of osteophyte formation. (Courtesy of Jeffrey A. Geller, MD, New York, NY.)
Seronegative Arthropathies
In general, these diseases are less severe than rheumatoid arthritis in severity and
complication risk.
Conditions such as psoriatic arthritis, which are associated with severe skin manifestations,
require special attention, especially on the day of surgical management, to decrease the risk of
PJI. If any skin lesions are present over the area of the planned surgical incision, strong
consideration should be given to postponing surgical management.
Similarly, patients with other conditions with systemic manifestations, such as systemic lupus
erythematosus, may present with renal abnormalities or other large organ system deficiencies
that lead to a higher rate of complications postoperatively.
Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
8/27

The mainstay of nonsurgical management is similar to that for primary osteoarthritis, including
physical therapy and/or periarticular injections; however, this classification of disease has
been categorically improved in the past 10 years with advances in medical treatments.
Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs have substantially reduced the amount of joint
degeneration requiring joint replacement surgery.
Surgical Management
Nonarthroplasty Techniques
A few nonarthroplasty surgical treatment options are available for these patients because they
typically present with end-stage degenerative changes if disease-modifying medications fail to
provide lasting relief.
Arthroplasty Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning in this generally delicate group of patients may be divided into medical
optimization and surgical planning.
Medical optimization
Surgical planning

Preoperative Planning
In patients who may be being treated with rheumatologic medications, surgeons must
determine whether/when patients need to discontinue these medications. The reason
for withholding these medications is that many of them are strong immunosuppressive
agents that may interfere with wound/incision healing potential. In general, only the
early-generation medications, such as methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, do not
need to be withheld for any period preoperatively. Most disease-modifying
antirheumatic drugs need to be withheld for at least 2 weeks preoperatively and not
restarted for at least 2 weeks postoperatively to ensure adequate healing of the skin
incisions and decreased risk of susceptibility to PJI. Similarly, patients being undergoing
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
9/27

long-term corticosteroid treatment may require intraoperative stress dosing because of
adrenal insufficiency (Resource 1).
Surgical planning for these patients should involve close, careful evaluation of bony
deformities, range of motion contractures, and bone stock. Similarly, degeneration of
the collateral ligaments leading to instability also must be ascertained preoperatively.
Understanding these possible deficiencies allows the surgeon to have various implant
options available at the time of surgery, if necessary. For example, having stems
available in case of poor bone quality or intraoperative fracture is prudent. The
availability of a prosthesis with varus-valgus constraint is be wise in the event that the
collateral ligaments have become attenuated.
Postoperative Management
Most postoperative protocols for these patients are not drastically different than those for
patients undergoing typical TKA.
Infection is the most feared complication in this patient population because they are
immunosuppressed and rely on medications that considerably increase their risk for wound
infection or PJI.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, 90% have cervical spine involvement. Patients with
rheumatoid arthritis should undergo dynamic cervical spine lateral flexion and extension
imaging before elective surgery to rule out atlantoaxial instability. A difference of more
than 9 to 10 mm in the atlanto-dens interval on flexion/extension views or less than 14
mm of space available for the spinal cord is associated with an increased risk of
neurologic injury and usually requires surgical management.
Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
10/27

Systemic complications
Infection
The risk of infection with total joint arthroplasty is increased in patients with psoriatic
arthritis.
Skin incision through active psoriatic lesions should be avoided because the lesions may be
highly colonized by bacteria.
Preoperative management of lesions in an incision area is recommended.
Complications in patients with ankylosing spondylitis
Patients with ankylosing spondylitis may have an increased risk for heterotopic ossification;
however, this risk is not supported by strong data.
These patients also have a greater risk for pulmonary complications because of chest wall
constriction and fibrotic changes.
Preoperative cardiopulmonary evaluation is recommended.
The rates of systemic complications, infection, revision, and 90-day readmission after TKA
in patients with different types of inflammatory arthritis were substantially higher than
those in control patients with osteoarthritis.
Outcomes
Although patients with inflammatory arthritis generally have a higher risk for complications,
many published studies detail nearly equivalent results based on patient-reported outcome
measures.
In most studies, patients with rheumatoid arthritis do not attain a functional outcome score as
high as patients without rheumatoid arthritis; however, pain relief and return to baseline
activities are similar.3
Oncologic Resection and Reconstruction
Background
Tumors around the knee
Improved survival

Background
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
11/27

Bone tumors are rare conditions and represent an exceedingly rare indication for TKA,
more commonly affecting young people. Malignant bone tumors represent
approximately 5% of all tumors in young people, with the knee and the proximal
humerus being the two most common locations of these tumors. Osteosarcoma is the
most common malignant bone tumor, and the distal femur and the proximal tibia are
the two most common sites for these tumors.
A more common benign oncologic process that leads to joint degeneration is pigmented
villonodular synovitis. In this process, aggressive hypertrophy of the synovial membrane
leads to a massive degenerative process, including repeated hemarthroses and cartilage
wear. If detected early, before joint degeneration, open or arthroscopic synovectomy can
be performed to help preserve the articular cartilage (Figure 4).
Advances in chemotherapy have led to improved survival rates in many patients with
malignant neoplasms affecting the knee, allowing limb salvage surgery to become the
standard of care for most patients.
Figure 4
Sagittal MRIs of a knee show pigmented villonodular synovitis. (Courtesy of Wakenda
Tyler, New York, NY.)
Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
12/27

Observation
Chemotherapy and radiation therapy

Nonsurgical Management
Benign tumors about the knee often are managed via monitoring only to determine
whether the tumor changes with time. During this period of observation, periodic
radiographs or other tests may be necessary. Some benign tumors can be managed
effectively via medications, whereas other tumors may disappear over time without
surgical management.
Certain bone tumors or metastatic diseases about the knee are amenable to nonsurgical
management via chemotherapy or radiation therapy if they do not compromise the
mechanical strength of the bone or the stability of the knee joint.
Surgical Management
Nonarthroplasty Techniques
Surgical excision or resection
Amputation

Nonarthroplasty Techniques
Some benign tumors about the knee can be removed via simple surgical excision with or
without local adjuvant treatment, such as cryotherapy, phenol, or bone cement. If
excision or curettage of the tumor compromises bone strength, stabilization with the
use of allograft and/or internal fixation techniques may be necessary to decrease the
risk of pathologic fracture. In addition, some extra-articular malignant tumors near the
knee also may be amenable to wide resection that can spare the knee joint.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
13/27

For pigmented villonodular synovitis, extensive débridement and synovectomy can be
performed to prevent further joint degeneration. In general, open synovectomy is
associated with a higher success rate in preventing further re-accumulation of synovium
compared with arthroscopic débridement; however, open management generally is
much more invasive with a slower recovery.
Above-the-knee amputation is preferred if the function of the limb cannot be maintained
or if the risk of metastasis is high.
Arthroplasty Techniques
For pigmented villonodular synovitis, reconstruction depends on the extent of disease. With
extensive joint degeneration but sparing of the collateral ligaments, a typical posterior-
stabilized component is the preferred treatment option. However, if damage or compromise
to the integrity of the collateral ligaments is present, a component with varus-valgus constraint
may lead to improved long-term stability and function.
Endoprosthetic reconstruction
High-demand patient population

Arthroplasty Techniques
Nonarthroplasty techniques are preferred if the function of the native knee joint can be
preserved; however, TKA is the preferred treatment option if the margin of resection will
compromise function of the knee. Segmental bone loss after wide resection of most of
these tumors typically requires reconstruction with the use of a modular endoprosthesis
rather than primary TKA components.
The improved survival that has resulted from better treatment options has strong
implications for arthroplasty techniques because many of these young patients will
continue to perform higher-demand activities than older patients who undergo TKA,
which will predispose them to mechanical failure of the endoprosthesis. Emphasis
should be placed on achieving reliable and durable fixation. If deficient or compromised

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028

bone is present or a prosthesis with varus/valgus constraint has been used, stem
fixation will be necessary.
Preoperative Planning
Selecting the appropriate implant system
Noncemented fixation
Anticipate future growth in skeletally immature patients

Preoperative Planning
Surgeons must anticipate bone loss after tumor resection and ensure that the
appropriate modular prosthetic reconstructive options are available to reconstruct this
bone loss. Most implant manufactures offer modular limb salvage endoprostheses.
Surgeons must understand these systems and select one that will meet the needs of the
patient.
Noncemented fixation generally is preferred in younger, high-demand patients with a
reasonable post-reconstruction life expectancy because of their potential for bone
ingrowth and to provide durable biologic fixation. Options for noncemented fixation
include long (eg, typically ≥150 mm) cylindrical or tapered press-fit stems or shorter (eg,
80 mm) dynamic compression fixation stems. Both offer good long-term fixation;
however, the latter can achieve fixation over a shorter segment of bone while minimizing
stress shielding and sealing the medullary canal from particulate debris and osteolysis.
Future growth for skeletally immature patients is an important consideration because
ide oncologic resection and endoprosthetic reconstruction inevitably will involve
resection of the growth plate. This is a challenging situation, and the treating surgeon
must consider ongoing growth of the contralateral limb to minimize current and future
leg-length discrepancy. Noninvasive expandable endoprostheses are a potential option
for children with a large expected leg-length discrepancy (eg, >3 cm) at skeletal maturity;

however, this treatment option is associated with a higher rate of mechanical
complications.
Postoperative Management
Oncologic needs
Weight-bearing precautions
Infection

Postoperative Management
The postoperative treatment of these patients typically is driven by their oncologic needs
more than the arthroplasty needs. Often, a desire exists to initiate chemotherapy or
radiation therapy as soon as the incision has healed.
Weight bearing may be modified or protected early postoperatively to allow for
osteointegration in patients with compromised bone if a cementless device has been
used. A typical postoperative protocol may include an initial 6 weeks of toe-touch weight
bearing, progressing to 50% weight bearing for an additional 6 weeks, and then
progressing to weight bearing as tolerated.
Infection prevention strategies should be maximized given the high risk of PJI in this
patient population.
Complications
High rate of complications

Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
16/27

A high rate of complications is noted in this patient population. The most common
complications are infections and mechanical failure, such as loosening or implant
fracture. Aseptic loosening is the most common long-term complication in tumor
endoprostheses.
Outcomes
Good outcomes can be achieved
Larger resections result in greater functional deficits

Outcomes
Multiple studies have reported achievement of good functional outcomes after
endoprosthetic reconstruction in this patient population if complications can be avoided
but with some degree of physical limitations compared with the contralateral limb.
Similar to patients undergoing primary TKA for other indications, patients undergoing
TKA with the use of a modular prosthesis for a tumor can expect to achieve progressive
functional improvements for 1 year postoperatively.
Surgeons must counsel patients that knee resection involves the wide loss of not only
bone but also many of the surrounding musculotendinous and ligamentous structures,
which may affect balance and neuromotor control of the knee. These functional deficits
are greater in patients who undergo wider resections of the distal femur and patients
who undergo treatment that involves the proximal tibia.
Osteonecrosis of the Knee
Background
Etiology
Diagnosis and evaluation
Differential diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty for Other Indications
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004028
17/27

Surgeons must not confuse osteonecrosis with similar knee disorders, such as
osteochondritis dissecans, transient osteoporosis, bone bruises, or occult fractures.
Osteochondritis dissecans is more common in the lateral aspect of the medial femoral
condyle of adolescent (age, 15 to 20 years) males.
Transient osteoporosis is more common in middle-aged men (age, 40 to 50 years) and
pregnant women. It is most common in the hip, followed by the knee and the foot or
ankle. Multiple joint involvement, referred to as transient migratory osteoporosis, is
present in approximately 40% of patients with transient osteoporosis.
Occult fractures and bone bruises generally are associated with trauma, bone fragility, or
overuse.
MRI characteristics

Background
Osteonecrosis of the knee may occur spontaneously (spontaneous osteonecrosis of the
knee [SPONK]) or secondary to an underlying disease or disorder, such as corticosteroid
use, trauma, or osteopenia. Regardless, osteonecrosis of the knee is a process similar to
osteonecrosis in other areas of the body in which some type of obstruction of the
vascularity to the medial or lateral femoral condyle occurs. Ultimately, the integrity of the
bony architecture and the condyle begins to collapse and resorb, leading to an
irregularity of the joint surface and subsequent collapse of the articular cartilage and
distraction of the joint as a result of the incongruities (Figure 5). If the disease is
extensive and leads to a very large area of distraction on the medial condyle and lack of
bony support, few alternative treatment options are available other than TKA. Secondary
osteonecrosis of the knee is much less common than osteonecrosis of the femoral head
(approximately 10%).
MRI is the most useful imaging modality for differentiating osteonecrosis from other
conditions. Bone edema observed on MRIs is a common feature of osteoarthritis,
osteonecrosis, cartilage injury, and transient regional osteoporosis. Serpentine lesions
within a well-demarcated border is an MRI finding specific for bone infarcts in the distal
femur.

Classification
Three distinct osteonecrosis pathologic entities with similar presentations exist.

Spontaneous Osteonecrosis of the Knee
SPONK is more common in women older than 55 years (Figure 6).
In 99% of patients, SPONK involves only one joint and only one condyle (typically, the medial
femoral condyle). Some evidence shows that these lesions represent microfractures.
Controversy exists with regard to whether SPONK is part of a progression of osteoarthritis or
an insufficiency fracture.

demonstrates spontaneous osteonecrosis in the medial condyle of the right knee. B, Sagittal T1-

courtesy of Thomas Parker Vail, MD, San Francisco, CA. Panel B reproduced from Mont MA,

162.)
Post-arthroscopic Osteonecrosis of the Knee
Associated with subchondral collapse
Usually involves the medial femoral condyle
The relationship to SPONK is unclear.
Secondary Osteonecrosis of the Knee
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:53 PM

Secondary osteonecrosis typically involves more than one compartment of the knee or the
metaphyseal bone.
Multifactorial etiology; characterized by loss of bone circulation.
Approximately 80% of patients have bilateral involvement, and many patients have multifocal
osteonecrosis.
Patients with secondary osteonecrosis typically are women (3:1 female-to-male ratio);
however, they usually are younger than 55 years and have associated risk factors for
osteonecrosis (Table 1).
Osteonecrotic lesions can occur in the epiphysis, diaphysis, or metaphysis.
Patients with secondary osteonecrosis should be clinically screened for other joint
involvement.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management includes analgesic agents (NSAIDs, tramadol), protected–weight
bearing, and physical therapy directed at quadriceps strengthening.
Good results have been demonstrated with nonsurgical management of SPONK and post-
arthroscopic osteonecrosis but not with secondary osteonecrosis.
Secondary osteonecrosis progresses to advanced osteoarthritis in 80% of patients treated
nonsurgically.
Although diphosphonates have been used to manage osteonecrosis of the hip with mixed
results, no evidence support the use of diphosphonates to manage osteonecrosis of the knee.
Surgical Management
Nonarthroplasty Techniques
SPONK and post-arthroscopic osteonecrosis
High tibial osteotomy if angular malalignment is present.
Bone grafting, osteochondral autograft transfer, osteochondral allografts, or mosaicplasty
are options if subchondral collapse is present.
Secondary osteonecrosis
Diagnostic arthroscopy (to remove small, unstable osteochondral fragments)
Core decompression (for lesions that do not involve the articular surface)
Osteochondral allograft (for larger compartmental lesions in younger patients)
Arthroplasty Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning in this patient population generally involves plain radiographs and MRIs.
Unicondylar Knee Arthroplasty

Unicondylar knee arthroplasty (UKA) is a good treatment option if a smaller total area of bone
is involved and only one condyle is involved.
TKA
TKA is preferred for larger lesions or bone collapse that precludes UKA. If a larger area of
damaged bone exists or more diffuse degenerative changes are present, TKA should be
considered over UKA. Similarly, if a deeper area of involvement of the affected condyle is
present, whereby bony support under the UKA components may not be adequate, TKA may be
a better option to help ensure longer term implant survivorship.
Postoperative Management
Similar to that already discussed in this lesson.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
In knees with large areas of osteonecrosis that may compromise fixation, the surgeon should
consider adding stems.
Complications
Infection, wound healing, and stiffness
Outcomes
Similar results as those reported for all patients who undergo TKA
Post-septic Arthritis of the Knee
Background
The incidence of this entity has declined with time.
Aggressive early surgical management with earlier irrigation and débridement has allowed for
preservation of joint function in more patients.
In the distant past, infections, such as tuberculosis infection of the hip, would lead to joint
destruction and the subsequent need for TKA.

Similarly, with the increased utility of arthroscopic management and broader spectrum
antibiotic agents, post-septic arthritis of the knee has become a rarer entity; however, it still
occurs.
The epidemiology of post-septic arthritis of the knee is quite rare.
Care must be taken to fully confirm the eradication of any sort of joint infection before
engaging in any type of arthroplasty procedure. If infection is not eradicated, catastrophic
failures may occur quite early in the postoperative period.
Nonsurgical Management
Principles of nonsurgical management, including medications and physical therapy, may be
used to manage post-septic arthritis of the knee.
One notable exception is that injections likely should be avoided in this patient population
because injections with corticosteroids or hyaluronic acid may lead to reactivation of the
infection if it has not been fully eradicated.
Surgical Management
Nonarthroplasty Techniques
Additional consideration should be given to nonarthroplasty treatment options in patients
with post-septic arthritis.
Interventions such as high tibial osteotomy for varus deformities versus distal femoral
osteotomies for valgus arthritis should be considered inpatients deemed to be at high risk for
TKA or if the patient is young.
Arthroplasty Techniques
Preoperative Planning
In general, surgeons should wait at least 12 months from the time of final clearance of septic
arthritis before considering TKA.
If the patient is free of any symptoms of infection after 1 year but severely debilitated by the
degenerative arthritis, surgeons must evaluate the patient again to confirm that the infection
has been eradicated.
Patients should undergo serologic testing for inflammatory markers (erythrocyte
sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein level) and definitive aspiration to rule out evidence

of continued infection as much as possible.
Cross-sectional imaging, such as MRI, may be performed in select patients to evaluate for
residual osteomyelitis or a small abscess. Surgical management should proceed only after as
much confirmatory evidence as possible shows that the previous infection has been
eradicated.
If any doubt exists with regard to residual or persistent infection, a two-stage procedure
should be considered. In the first stage, primary bone cuts for placement of TKA are made,
with placement of an articulating high-dose antibiotic cement spacer. This is followed by a 6-
week course of intravenous antibiotic agents, and subsequent TKA on completion of the
intravenous antibiotic agents.
Postoperative Management
Postoperatively, these patients may be treated similar to patients undergoing typical TKA.
Consideration may be given to a 3-month course of oral antibiotic agents, which is similar to
that for patients who have undergone two-stage removal and reimplantation after PJI.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Similar to traditional TKA, with the added consideration of an additional 3 months of oral
antibiotic agents after reimplantation.
Careful follow-up is necessary for to maintain close surveillance of the surgical incision and
soft tissues for another infection.
Complications
Similar to that of traditional TKA, with the added vigilance for postoperative PJI.

Outcomes
Few reports have been published on the success of TKA in patients with septic arthritis
of the native knee. In one of the largest series, which compared one-stage and two-stage
procedures for definitive management, both approaches resulted in an excellent
outcome with regards to recurrence of infection. At final follow-up, 26 of 30 patients
were aseptic after a two-stage procedure for evolutive infection, and 22 of 23 patients
